sections.h: Israel, my servant, chosen and not rejected (Isaiah 41:8–10)
sections.b: The servant first appears by name: "But you, Israel, my servant, / Jacob, whom I have chosen, / offspring of Abraham, who loved me" (41:8). Here the servant is plainly the nation, the descendants of Abraham, whom God "grasped from the ends of the earth" and told, "I chose you, and I never rejected you" (41:9). The title is an honor: in the Bible "my servant" is used of Abraham, Moses, David and the prophets. Spoken to exiles who thought God had cast them off, it answers their fear directly. The assurance that follows ("Don't be afraid, because I am with you", 41:10) uses the form of an oracle of salvation, and its promise of strength is given to a people who feel like a "worm" (41:14).

"Look at my servant! I hold him up. / He is my chosen one; my soul is pleased with him" (42:1). This servant is not named. God puts his Spirit on him, and his task is to "bring justice out to the nations", but gently: he will not shout, snap a crushed reed or put out a dim wick, and he himself will not burn dim or be crushed (42:2–4, a play on the same two verbs). In 42:6–7 God makes him "a covenant of the people / and a light to the nations", to open blind eyes and free prisoners. The Greek writes "Jacob" and "Israel" into 42:1; the Targum has "my servant the Messiah"; medieval Jewish commentators divide (Rashi: Israel; Ibn Ezra: the prophet; Kimchi and Abarbanel: the King Messiah); Matthew quotes the whole song of Jesus' quiet ministry of healing (Matthew 12:18–21), and the baptism voice echoes 42:1 (Matthew 3:17). Since Duhm (1892) these verses have been counted as the first of four "servant songs".

Straight after the song comes its opposite: "Who is blind, if not my servant? / Who is deaf like the messenger I send?" (42:19). Israel, called to open blind eyes, is itself blind, and its exile is explained as the result of refusing to listen to God's teaching (42:24). This contrast is one of the main reasons many readers distinguish the servant of 42:1–9 from Israel as it actually was: the ideal servant does what the real nation failed to do. Others see the same Israel described first by its calling and then by its condition.

"You are my witnesses, the LORD declares, / and my servant, whom I chose" (43:10). The line may describe one group by two titles, the people as both witnesses and servant, or two witnesses: the people, and a servant who is distinct from them. Most interpreters take the first view. The Targum reads "my servant the Messiah", as at 42:1. The purpose is stated: "so that you will know and trust me / and grasp that I am he". The servant's first task here is to know God and testify to him.

sections.h: Jacob my servant, shaped from the womb (Isaiah 44:1–2, 21)
sections.b: Chapter 44 calls Israel the servant three times. God is the one "who shaped you from the womb" (44:2), language later used of the individual servant of 49:1 and 49:5, and he promises to pour his Spirit on the servant's children (44:3). In 44:21 Israel is told, "Keep these things in mind ... for you are my servant. / I shaped you; you are my own servant. / Israel, you will not be forgotten by me." The repetition ties the servant title to creation and election: God made Israel for this role, and will not forget it, even after the failure described in 42:18–25 and 43:22–28.

common: In Isaiah 41:8–9, 44:1–2 and 44:21 the servant is plainly Israel; the debate is over 42:1–9 and the later songs.
The New Testament applies the first servant song to Jesus (Matthew 12:18–21).
uncommon: A few scholars have proposed that 42:1–7 first described Cyrus, who is also 'called in righteousness' (42:6; 45:13).
The messianic reading of 42:1 runs from the Targum ('my servant the Messiah') through Kimchi and Abarbanel, beside Rashi's reading of Israel, Ibn Ezra's of the prophet and Saadia Gaon's of Cyrus.

sections.h: The man from the east, named at last (Isaiah 41–44)
sections.b: Isaiah 41 twice speaks of a conqueror without naming him: "Who has roused a man from the east / and calls him in righteousness to his service?" (41:2), and "From the north I have roused a man, and here he comes" (41:25). Kings and nations fall before him (41:2–3), and the gods of the nations cannot say who sent him. Only in 44:28 does God name him: "who says of Cyrus, 'My shepherd! / He will do all that I please'", and the task is to say that Jerusalem will be rebuilt and the temple founded. The title "shepherd" was used of kings, David above all (2 Samuel 5:2). Cyrus came from Persia, east of Babylon, and ruled Media to the north, which fits both directions. The Targum and Rashi read 41:2 of Abraham instead. How 44:28 came to name Cyrus is the central question of the book's authorship; the chapter page for Isaiah 44 sets out both views.

Isaiah 40–48 mocks idols more than any other part of the Bible. The pattern is set in 40:18–20: a smith casts the image and plates it with gold, and a poorer man picks wood that will not rot and hires a craftsman so it "will not tip over". In 41:6–7 the craftsmen cheer each other on and nail the god in place. The longest satire is 44:9–20: an ironworker grows faint with hunger as he forges, a carpenter gives his block the "form of a man", and a man burns half a log to bake bread and prays to the other half, "Rescue me! You are my god." The point is made in the narrator's verdict: "He cannot rescue his own life" (44:20). Babylonian rites claimed that the gods, not the craftsmen, made the statue; the satire deliberately describes only the craftsmen. The same argument runs through Psalm 115:4–8, Jeremiah 10:1–16 and Wisdom of Solomon 13:10–19.

common: Isaiah 44:9–20 is the Bible's most detailed mockery of idol-making.
uncommon: Some scholars think the satire was a separate prose piece set into the poems later.

sections.h: "Except for me there is no god" (Isaiah 43–44)
sections.b: Isaiah 40–48 contains the Bible's most explicit statements that only one God exists. "No god was shaped before me, / and none will exist after me" (43:10); "I am first, and I am last, / and except for me there is no god" (44:6); "Is there a God apart from me? / No, there is no rock. I know none" (44:8). Earlier texts often affirm that Israel must worship the LORD alone (Exodus 20:3) or that he is above all gods (Psalm 95:3). These chapters go further and deny that other gods are gods at all, and they argue for it: the LORD alone created the world (40:26; 44:24), alone announced events before they happened (41:21–29; 44:7), and alone saves (43:11). Scholars often treat these chapters as a turning point in the history of monotheism; others hold that Deuteronomy 4:35 and 32:39 already say the same.

Isaiah 40–55 pictures the return from Babylon as a second exodus. It begins with a road for the LORD in the wilderness (40:3). God makes water flow in the desert and plants trees there (41:17–20). He is the one who "opened a road in the sea" and put out Pharaoh's army "like a wick" (43:16–17), and then he says, "Stop calling the earlier things to mind ... Look at me, about to do something new": a road and rivers in the wilderness (43:18–20). In 44:27 he says to the deep, "Dry up!" Israel passes through water and fire unharmed (43:2), and Egypt is named as the ransom paid (43:3). The pattern continues in 48:20–21, 51:9–11 and 52:11–12, and the Gospels take it up when John the Baptist appears in the wilderness.

After chapter 39 ends with the warning that Hezekiah's treasures and descendants will be carried to Babylon, chapter 40 opens: "Comfort, comfort my people". Isaiah's name, Hezekiah and the Assyrian crisis disappear; the hearers are addressed as people whose punishment is over, and Babylon, Cyrus and the return come into view. This is why most scholars since Döderlein (1775) and Duhm (1892) assign 40–55 to a prophet of the exile, while traditional readers (Allis, Young, Motyer, Oswalt) hold that Isaiah wrote them for a future generation, as Ben Sira already believed (Sirach 48:24–25). Recent work stresses how 40:1–11 answers the call of 6:1–13 and continues the book's themes, such as "the Holy One of Israel". The chapter pages for Isaiah 40 and 44 give the arguments.

"A voice calls out: / In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" (40:3). All four Gospels apply the verse to John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:2–3; Luke 3:4–6; John 1:23). In John's Gospel he says it of himself: "I am a voice of someone shouting in the wilderness" (John 1:23). The Gospels follow the Greek, which links "in the wilderness" with the voice, while the Hebrew links it with the road. The Qumran community quoted the same verse to explain its own withdrawal to the desert (Community Rule, 1QS 8:12–16). Luke continues the quotation through 40:5, ending with the Greek's promise that all flesh will see God's salvation.

The family title go'el, the relative who buys back land or a family member sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:25, 25:47–49) and the one who avenges a killing (Numbers 35:19), becomes one of the main titles of God in Isaiah 40–66. It first appears in 41:14: "The Holy One of Israel is your redeemer." In 43:1 God says, "Don't be afraid. I have redeemed you", and in 43:3 he names a price: "I hand over Egypt as your ransom." In 44:6 and 44:24 "your redeemer" introduces God's great claims, and in 44:22–23 redemption is announced as already done. The image tells the exiles that God claims them as family and will pay what it costs to free them.

sections.h: "I am first, and I am last" in Isaiah
sections.b: The phrase behind Revelation's "the First and the Last" comes from Isaiah, where it is the LORD's own claim. In 41:4 it is "I, the LORD, am first, / and with the last ones I am he"; in 44:6, "I am first, and I am last, / and except for me there is no god"; and in 48:12 it returns once more. In Isaiah the point is that God exists before history begins and after it ends, and directs everything in between, so no other god can claim to have caused or foreseen events. Revelation applies the title to the risen Jesus (Revelation 1:17; Revelation 2:8) and joins it to "the Alpha and the Omega" (Revelation 22:13). Churches differ on what that implies; see the card on the Isaiah 44 page.

The opening of Isaiah 40 has plural commands ("Comfort, comfort") and unnamed voices ("A voice calls out", "A voice says"). Many scholars, following Frank Moore Cross (1953), hear in it a meeting of the LORD's heavenly council, like 1 Kings 22:19–22 and Isaiah 6, where God's decisions are passed to his attendants and a prophet overhears or is sent. In 40:6 the prophet answers, "What shall I call out?" (following the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek). 40:13–14 then denies that God needs any adviser in such a council: "What adviser of his has taught him anything?" The Targum turns the plural into "prophets", and the Greek adds "priests".

The prophet is told to call out that "All flesh is grass": human beings wither when the LORD's wind blows on them, "but our God's word will stand forever" (40:8). The word here is God's promise of comfort and return, which outlasts the powers of the day. The theme returns at the end of 40–55: God's word goes out like rain and does not return empty (55:10–11). 1 Peter 1:24–25 quotes 40:6–8 in its Greek form and calls the word "the good news" that was preached. In the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek, part of 40:7–8 is missing; see the variants.

sections.h: The Spirit on the servant and on Israel's children (Isaiah 42:1; 44:3)
sections.b: Isaiah 40–44 speaks of God's Spirit three ways. In 40:13 no one has "taken the measure of the LORD's Spirit": the Spirit is God's own mind and power in creation. In 42:1 God says of his servant, "I have placed my Spirit on him", as on the shoot of Jesse (11:2), equipping him for his task; Matthew applies this to Jesus (Matthew 12:18). In 44:3 the gift is for a whole generation: "On your children I will pour out my Spirit", like water on dry ground. The same promise appears in Ezekiel 36:26–27, Ezekiel 39:29 and Joel 2:28–29, which Peter quotes at Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and Jesus' promise of living water is explained as the Spirit (John 7:37–39).

Isaiah 40–44 is full of the nations: they are a drop in a bucket to God (40:15), they are summoned to court (41:1; 43:9), and their gods are mocked. Yet the servant's task is to "bring justice out to the nations" (42:1), and the far islands "are waiting for his teaching" (42:4). God makes him "a light to the nations" (42:6), and the whole earth is called to sing a new song (42:10–12). In 44:5 people say, "I am the LORD's", and "take Israel as an honored name"; many readers, Jewish and Christian, have seen converts from the nations here. The New Testament takes up the "light to the nations" for Jesus and for the church's mission to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47).

sections.h: The shepherd God and the shepherd king (Isaiah 40:11; 44:28)
sections.b: "Like a shepherd he will graze his flock" (40:11): the God who comes "in strength" (40:10) gathers the lambs in his arms and carries them in the fold of his robe, and guides the ewes that are nursing. The picture is tender, fitted to a people facing a long journey home. In 44:28 God calls Cyrus "My shepherd", using the royal title given to David (2 Samuel 5:2; Psalm 78:70–72). The Bible's shepherd language, for God (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34) and for Jesus (John 10:11), draws on both ideas: care for the weak and rule over the flock.

claude.title: Ashes and a shepherd
claude.body: In 44:20 the idol-worshiper 'grazes on ashes' (ro'eh 'efer), and eight verses later God calls Cyrus 'my shepherd' (ro'i), from the same root. I suspect the echo is deliberate: the chapter sets a man who herds nothing but the ashes of his own fire against a king who 'shepherds' at God's word and rebuilds Jerusalem. It is a possibility, not something the text states.

sections.b: The promises of Isaiah 41–44 are addressed to "Israel, my servant, / Jacob, whom I have chosen" (41:8), and "I chose you, and I never rejected you" (41:9) is a key verse for the question of whether God's choice of Israel still stands. Jewish readers take the promises as Israel's. Christian traditions differ: some apply them to the church as the new or true Israel in Christ; some hold that they still belong to the Jewish people, who remain chosen (compare Romans 11:28–29); many hold both. The card on the Isaiah 41 page sets out the main views.

Isaiah 40–55 argues from creation more than any other prophet. God measured the oceans in his palm (40:12), "created these" stars and calls each by name (40:26), and "created the far edges of the earth" without tiring (40:28). He "created the heavens and stretched them out" and "hammered out the earth" (42:5), and in 44:24 he is the one "who stretched out the heavens alone, / who hammered out the earth (who was with me?)". The verbs bara' (create), yatsar (shape) and 'asah (make) are used of the world and of Israel alike (43:1, 7, 15). Creation is not a separate doctrine here but the ground of hope: the one who made everything can remake his people's future.

These chapters are rich in titles. God is "the Holy One of Israel" (41:14, 16, 20; 43:3, 14), the title that runs through the whole book; "the Holy One" alone in 40:25; "the King of Jacob" (41:21) and "the King of Israel" (44:6); "your redeemer" (41:14; 43:14; 44:6, 24); "the God of the ages" (40:28); "the LORD of Armies" (44:6); and "rock" (44:8). He speaks of himself as "I am he" (41:4; 43:10, 13) and "first ... and last" (41:4; 44:6). Each title answers a fear of the exiles: holy and therefore just, king when they have none, kin who will buy them back, and the one who was there before Babylon's gods and will be there after them.

From chapter 43 Babylon is named as the power God is about to bring down: "For your sake I am sending to Babylon. / I will bring them all down as runaways, / the Chaldeans, in the ships they used to cheer" (43:14). Its diviners and fortune-tellers will be made fools (44:25), and some read God's word to the deep, "Dry up! / I will dry out your rivers" (44:27), as a hint of the Euphrates, Babylon's river; Greek historians later said Cyrus drained it to enter the city. The Babylonian Chronicle reports that Cyrus's army entered Babylon without a battle in 539 BC. Chapters 46–47 then describe Babylon's gods carried off and the city humbled.

The Hebrew 'ani hu', "I (am) he", is a short, emphatic way for the LORD to identify himself: "I, the LORD, am first, / and with the last ones I am he" (41:4); "so that you will know and trust me / and grasp that I am he" (43:10); "Since the first day, I am he" (43:13). It appears first in Deuteronomy 32:39. The Greek translates it egō eimi, "I am", the words Jesus uses absolutely in John's Gospel, as in "unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins" (John 8:24) and "so that when it comes to pass you will believe that I am" (John 13:19). John 13:19 closely echoes Isaiah 43:10, where God's announcing events in advance is the ground for believing.

"Like a thick cloud I have wiped away your rebellions, / like a cloud, your sins. / Turn back to me. I have redeemed you" (44:22). The order is unusual: forgiveness and redemption are announced first, and the call to return (shuv, the Bible's word for repentance) rests on them. 43:25 says the same, "I myself, I am the one / who wipes away your rebellions for my own sake", directly after a list of Israel's failures. In other prophets repentance often comes as the condition of mercy (Jeremiah 18:7–8; Joel 2:12–14); here mercy comes first and makes return possible.
